reader_summary: I understand this section as a decision about which trained assistant to keep. Different post-training methods accept different teaching signals, so they are choices to combine according to a goal rather than compulsory successive stations. Here two answers to the same calculator question both preserve the fact 9; the chosen answer is shorter and the rejected answer adds a greeting. A DPO branch compares an updating policy against a separately frozen copy of the joint starting model. The local Python example uses random equal starting weights only to demonstrate the zero relative preference margin and the gradient switches; it is not the reported joint checkpoint or a training run. The reported branch trained with a mixture of DPO, demonstration loss and expert-load balancing, yet the short-answer score stayed 3/3 while joint image/audio performance fell from 18/18 to 14/18 and the total fell from 75/84 to 71/84. That makes retaining joint as the recommended MoE model understandable. A student trained from the other branch follows that branch as its teacher, so it is a separate comparison. The exercise checks the policy gradient flag instead of the reference flag and should change False to True without updating either model.

Those links establish the teaching signals, fixed reference, factual preference design, expert routing and joint continuation. To understand the whole-sequence length comparison, beta and the 0.6931 baseline, I followed 13.4 to 13.3 and 13.6, then 13.6 to 13.5. Their exact raw snapshots and source hashes are saved. The optional PPO branch and later deployment comparison are labelled as separate work and are not needed to follow the current argument. The section is not the first numbered section, so no chapter introduction receipt applies.

terminology.details: SFT learns demonstrated answers; DPO adjusts the relative preference between two answers; RLHF names a learning flow using human feedback, while PPO names an update method. The section defines joint, MoE, Dense, the capability matrix and expert-routing balance. The linked MoE section makes an expert a stored feed-forward rule set, not a separate assistant. Reference means the frozen starting copy and policy means the model being updated; the synthetic pairs are explicitly distinguished from human labels. DIRECT: is explicitly an action prefix. The permitted DPO links explain whole-answer log probability, beta as a positive score-scaling setting, sigmoid and gradient flags. No remaining undefined term prevents my understanding of this section.

examples.details: The question is explicitly printed as 原題：3+6。計算器回報：9。請回答。. Both DIRECT:9 and DIRECT:9，祝你愉快！ contain the same answer 9, so their preference isolates concision rather than a change of fact. Equal policy/reference starts make each model’s chosen-minus-rejected log-score gap identical, so subtracting them yields zero. From the linked loss L=-log(sigmoid(beta×margin)), margin=0 gives -log(0.5)=0.6931. The larger experiment is clearly cited rather than rerun: 100 updates use beta 0.1, demonstration-loss coefficient 0.2 and route-balance coefficient 0.01. A first-batch loss about 0.6931 and last-batch loss about 0.0000460 are explicitly different batches, which prevents treating their difference as a fixed-test improvement. Unchanged 3/3 short-answer generation and decreases of four correct answers in both the 18-question joint task and 84-question total explain the choice of joint weights.

program_explanation.details: torch.manual_seed(42) fixes the illustrative random start. build_dataset() returns splits and a manifest that this code ignores with _. preference_pairs(splits["train"])[0] selects the first pair made only from training rows, and pair["row"]["user"] prints the shared prompt. CapstoneModel() constructs the random policy; frozen_reference(policy) makes its separate non-updating copy. preference_loss(policy, reference, [pair]) computes one pair’s DPO loss and returns additional information ignored by _. The selected/rejected strings let me check the same prompt and fact. loss.item() extracts the scalar and round(...,4) prints four decimal places. any(p.requires_grad for p in reference.parameters()) asks whether even one reference parameter has its gradient flag enabled. I predicted and actually observed loss 0.6931 and False in an offline CPU process. No backward call, optimizer step or checkpoint loading occurs in this example.

exercise.details: The exercise specifies both substitutions: inspect policy.parameters() and display policy可更新. A new policy has gradient flags enabled, so any(...) becomes True; the independently frozen reference remains False. Merely changing the displayed text would leave the object being inspected unchanged. I saved this prediction before execution, ran the exact requested two substitutions in a new offline CPU process, and observed the same prompt, preference strings and 0.6931 loss with policy可更新 True. This checks the flag only and does not train the policy.
